statement: In people who used ketamine frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether lower memory and thinking scores fade after they cut down or stop, and the question is contested. People who had stopped scored no lower than people who did not use ketamine: 30 people abstinent for at least a month by their own account (a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980, although their hair, covering about the previous 3 months, held some ketamine on average) did not differ on any test from 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs (Morgan et al., 2009), and the 23 or 24 of them retested a year later (the paper's tables and text differ), 3 of whom had resumed at least monthly use, again showed no deficits (Morgan et al., 2010b); but they were different people from the frequent group and had used less before stopping (2.55 days a month just before stopping and a group peak of 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13), although 12 had once used frequently and 8 daily and the group had used ketamine for more years (7.63 against 6.07), so these comparisons cannot show recovery, as the authors themselves state. In the only study that retested a group of people who had cut down (Morgan et al., 2004a), 18 of the 57 ketamine participants of two earlier field studies (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down how often they used (from a mean of 6.45 to 1.61 days a month, although the amount they reported taking per occasion rose; 8 had not used for more than 6 months), were retested 3 to 4 years after a session held 3 days after a night of use, beside 10 polydrug controls: their lower category fluency no longer differed (group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032), a gain the authors report as correlated with the reduction in use (r = 0.712) and, as strongly, with time since last use (r = 0.723); but immediate story recall and digit-cancellation speed (66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 seconds) were lower at both sessions with no reported change, delayed recall was lower overall while the controls' fell at follow-up, and sentence judging was lower across both sessions although it appeared to improve, which fits differences that were there before as well as lasting effects, as the authors concede for story recall; the authors also note that the participants from the second field study were already slower on the attention task at the first session. People who were still using a year later (22 of 25 at least monthly; 20.08 days a month for all 30 at the first session, 16.0 for the 25 at follow-up) had better mean scores on spatial working memory (errors 29.58 to 19.92) and pattern recognition (83.68% to 89.04%), changes the paper did not test, and significantly better strategy and planning scores (P = 0.003 each), which the authors attribute partly to practice on tasks with only one version and to a poor start; their reported correlations between change in amount and change in errors and pattern recognition (r = 0.623 and −0.732) are weaker in the plotted points (about 0.55 and −0.55, editors' calculation). Letter fluency fell over the year in the abstinent and frequent groups, and also in both control groups. All the evidence comes from one research group, with self-reported use. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Nobody knows yet whether the memory differences seen in people who use ketamine most days go away after they cut down or stop. In one London team's studies, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month, most of them for many months, did as well on memory and thinking tests as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But they were different people, most of whom had used less before stopping, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything. The only study that followed a group who had cut down retested 18 people: after 3 to 4 years, one word test had caught up with the comparison group, while story memory and speed stayed lower, as they had been at the first test. That could mean lasting effects, or differences that were there before they started. People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, partly perhaps from practice.
population: People who used ketamine frequently and then stopped or cut down, studied by one research group at University College London: an ex-ketamine group of 30 (23 or 24 retested a year later, by the paper's tables and text) and 18 people from two earlier field studies who had cut down, retested after 3 to 4 years
exposure: Stopping ketamine (abstinent for at least a month, a mean of 344 days) or cutting down (from a mean of 6.45 to 1.61 days a month)
comparator: People who used other drugs but not ketamine and people who used no illicit drugs, tested at the same times; people who still used ketamine frequently
outcome: Memory and thinking test scores after stopping or cutting down, and their change over time
magnitude: Ex-ketamine group (Morgan et al., 2009; 30 people, abstinent a mean of 344.43 days, range 120–2980, hair ketamine 3.55 (13.63) ng/mm; 2.55 days a month before stopping, peak 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13): no differences from 30 polydrug and 30 non-drug controls on any test; 23 or 24 retested a year later, 3 again using at least monthly: no deficits at either session (Morgan et al., 2010b). Morgan et al. (2004a), 18 who had cut down (6.45 to 1.61 days a month, the self-reported amount per occasion rising) against 10 polydrug controls, 3–4 years apart: category fluency group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032 (first session t = 2.42, P = 0.023; no difference at follow-up); change in category fluency with change in use r = 0.712 and with time since last use r = 0.723; story recall group F(1,26) = 4.36 (immediate) and 4.43 (delayed); digit cancellation 66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 s; sentences judged group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007. Frequent group over a year (22 of 25 still using at least monthly; Morgan et al., 2010b): errors 29.58 to 19.92 and pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (mean changes, not tested); strategy 31.63 to 27.33 and Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (P = 0.003 each); correlations with change in amount r = 0.623 and −0.732 as printed, about 0.55 and −0.55 from the plotted points (editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Method › Participants (p. 78); Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 2nd paragraph (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
evidence.extracted: The ex-ketamine group (30 people, abstinent for at least 1 month) had been abstinent for 344.43 (624.72) days on average (range 120–2980); just before stopping it had used ketamine on 2.55 (3.90) days a month, with a group peak of 11.21 (9.34) days a month, against the frequent group's current 20.13 (2.36); 12 had previously used frequently and 8 daily, and its years of ketamine use were 7.63 (2.63) against 6.07 (4.89) in the frequent group.

evidence.locator: Figures 1 and 2 (pp. 82–83); Table 5 (p. 83); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 84, continuing on p. 85) and Neurocognitive function, 3rd paragraph (p. 85)
evidence.extracted: The authors report no differences between the ex-ketamine group and the polydrug and non-drug controls on any neuropsychological test (for example Stockings problems 8.89 (1.40) against 9.53 and 9.30; word recognition d′ 2.97 (0.63) against 2.85 and 2.67), and infer that the frequent group's impairments may be reversible on stopping, noting that 8 of the ex-ketamine group had once used ketamine daily and that the group had used ketamine for longer than the other ketamine groups. Editors' reading of Figures 1 and 2: the ex-ketamine group made the fewest spatial working-memory errors (about 11) and had the highest pattern recognition (about 94%).

The authors acknowledge that comparing the frequent and ex-ketamine groups cannot show reversibility, and that the only way to conclude that deficits reverse after stopping would be to retest the frequent group after a sufficient period of abstinence.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Participants and design, last paragraph (p. 122); Discussion › Reversibility of impairments, 1st paragraph (p. 131)
evidence.extracted: 24 of the 30 in the abstinent group were retested after about a year. The authors found no improvement in that group's cognitive function as abstinence continued, but also no cognitive deficits against either control group at the first session or at follow-up; they suggest the group had already recovered, while stating that their data cannot address the question, and call for prospective studies that follow people into abstinence.
evidence.quote: these data cannot really speak to this issue

evidence.extracted: At follow-up 3 of the 23 in the abstinent group were again using ketamine at least monthly; days since last use at follow-up are given as 540.54 (691.19) in the text but 34.71 (50.49), range 0–140, in Table 2, and the analyses keep the five original groups.

evidence.locator: Method, 1st paragraph (p. 1452); Results › Drug use (Table 2), 3rd paragraph (p. 1454)
evidence.extracted: Of the 76 people in two earlier field studies, 33 could be contacted and all but 2 agreed, 19 of them from the ketamine groups; after excluding one person who had developed schizophrenia and two controls who had started using ketamine, 18 people from the ketamine groups and 10 polydrug controls were retested 3 to 4 years after the drug-free session held 3 days after a night of use. Reported ketamine use had fallen from a mean of 6.45 (8.13) to 1.61 (3.19) days a month (described as an average reduction of 88.3%), and 8 had not used ketamine for more than 6 months.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1450); Results › Cognitive tasks › Semantic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1454, continuing on p. 1455); Table 3, Figure 1 and Speed of comprehension task, 1st paragraph (p. 1455); Correlations, 1st paragraph (p. 1457)
evidence.extracted: Category fluency showed a group × time interaction (F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032): the ketamine group named fewer category members at the first session (t = 2.42, P = 0.023) but not at follow-up; errors on sentence judging differed at the first session (1.06 (1.12) against 0.2 (0.42)) but not at follow-up (0.38 against 0.4), when they were at floor (interaction F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047); the change in category fluency (follow-up minus first score) correlated with the change in ketamine use (r = 0.712) and with time since last use (r = 0.723), and the abstract describes the improvement as correlated with the reduction in use. Editors' reading of Figure 1: about 16 against 21 category members at the first session and about 20 against 21 at follow-up; the sign convention for change in use is not stated (card sc_morgan_2004a).

evidence.locator: Results › Speed of comprehension task, 1st paragraph (p. 1455); Episodic memory, 1st paragraph, and Digit cancellation, 1st paragraph (p. 1456); Discussion › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1458)
evidence.extracted: Sentences judged were fewer in the ketamine group across both sessions (group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007); story recall was lower across both sessions (immediate F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047; delayed F(1,26) = 4.43, P = 0.045), with no group × time result reported and with the controls' delayed recall falling at follow-up; digit cancellation was slower at both sessions, 66.01 (14.12) and 65.32 (11.34) seconds against 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74), without more errors. The authors say the persisting episodic-memory deficit could be due either to pre-existing differences or to ketamine use. Editors' reading of Figures 2 and 3: about 62 against 86 sentences at the first session and 73 against 83 at follow-up; delayed recall about 7.2 against 9.7 idea units at the first session and 7.4 against 8.2 at follow-up.

None of the 18 had escalated or kept the same level of use. The authors state that the 38 members of the original ketamine group who could not be contacted may have continued using ketamine, that a group continuing ketamine use would have been the right comparison, that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out without prospective studies, and that retrospective estimates of drug use are inevitably inaccurate and could not be checked objectively. Editors' calculation: 19 re-contacted and 38 not contacted give 57 original ketamine participants, of whom 18 (32%) were analysed.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 125); Results › Cognitive assessments (Table 3) › Spatial Working Memory task › Strategy, and Stockings of Cambridge task (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127); Discussion › Cognitive function, 2nd paragraph (p. 131)
evidence.extracted: The frequent group, 22 of 25 still using ketamine at least monthly at follow-up (16.0 (10.01) days a month against 20.08 (7.41) for all 30 at the first session), had better mean scores over the year: spatial working-memory errors 29.58 (19.93) to 19.92 (17.56) and pattern recognition 83.68% (10.27) to 89.04% (7.24), for which only group main effects are reported (no test of change), against 88.41% (polydrug) and 89.58% (non-drug) at follow-up, strategy 31.63 (5.31) to 27.33 (6.33) (P = 0.003) and Stockings 7.67 (1.74) to 9.50 (1.89) (P = 0.003), inside the other groups' follow-up range (9.33 to 9.87); averaged over both sessions it still made more errors than all other groups (group F(4,108) = 4.16) and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups (printed F(1,108) = 4.429). The authors attribute the strategy and planning improvements partly to practice, since these tasks have only one version, and to the group's poor first scores leaving more room to improve.

evidence.locator: Results › Correlations between change in amount of ketamine use and other measures in frequent users (Fig. 2), 1st paragraph (p. 129); Figure 2 (p. 130)
evidence.extracted: Change in self-reported amount of ketamine over the year correlated with change in spatial working-memory errors (r = 0.623, P = 0.004) and with change in pattern recognition (r = −0.732, P < 0.001); the text says the current ketamine-using groups, the heading and the figure legend the frequent group. Editors' calculation from the coordinates of the plotted points in the PDF's vector drawing: r ≈ 0.55 (22 points, P ≈ 0.008) and r ≈ −0.55 (25 points, P ≈ 0.004), and the plotted changes in errors average about +12 although Table 3 shows the group's errors falling by 9.66, so the axis conventions of panel A cannot be read literally (card sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issues).

evidence.locator: Table 3 (p. 127); Results › Fluency › Verbal fluency (p. 128); Discussion › Cognitive function, 1st paragraph (p. 131)
evidence.extracted: Letter fluency showed a time × group interaction (F(4,108) = 2.84, P = 0.027), with lower scores at follow-up in the frequent (P = 0.046) and abstinent groups (P = 0.023), which the authors describe as a possible progressive decline; in Table 3 letter fluency fell from 16.38 to 13.48 (frequent) and 17.36 to 15.12 (abstinent), and also in the polydrug (17.33 to 15.25) and non-drug controls (16.32 to 14.53).

As summarized by the review (second-hand, by two of the same authors): memory impairments may be reversible when people stop using ketamine, since they were not found in a group of 30 people who had stopped using ketamine and been abstinent for at least a year (no reference given). Editors' note: the ex-ketamine group of 30 in Morgan et al. (2009) had been abstinent for 120 to 2980 days, so if the review means that group, at least a year does not match the primary paper.

evidence.locator: Method, 1st paragraph (p. 1452); Results › Drug use (Table 2), 3rd paragraph (p. 1454); Discussion › Attention and working memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1458)
evidence.extracted: While the number of days of ketamine use had fallen, the self-reported mean amount per occasion rose from 0.31 (0.25) g at the first session to 0.44 (0.97) g at follow-up (p. 1454). The authors note that the participants drawn from Curran & Monaghan (2001) had poorer attentional functioning at the first session than the ketamine group of Curran & Morgan (2000), whose study had found no attentional difference from its controls 3 days after use (p. 1458); the 10 controls came from the original polydrug control group (p. 1452), and how many of the 18 came from each earlier study is not stated.

evidence.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 1st paragraph (p. 80); Table 2, ex-users column (p. 81)
evidence.extracted: Hair samples (3 cm, about the previous 3 months) were analysed for ketamine. The ex-ketamine group, whose shortest reported abstinence was 120 days (range 120–2980), had a mean hair ketamine level of 3.55 (13.63) ng/mm, while none was detected in either control group; the paper does not comment on this or give a threshold for classifying participants by hair.

risk_of_bias.note: Selection: the 3-year follow-up kept 18 of 57 original ketamine participants, all of whom had cut down, and excluded the one who had developed schizophrenia; testers knew the groups; use and abstinence were self-reported (hair results only for the one-year cohort, in which the abstinent group's hair held some ketamine on average and its days since last use are contradictory); the abstinent group was not reclassified when 3 of 23 resumed monthly use (cards sc_morgan_2004a: ROBINS-E very high; sc_morgan_2009 and sc_morgan_2010b: high).

inconsistency.note: Category fluency caught up after cutting down while story recall and speed did not; people who had stopped showed no deficits, while people who cut down kept some; reported correlations are weaker in the plotted data.

indirectness.note: The question is whether the same people recover; most of the evidence compares different people (those who had stopped, who had used less, against those still using), and the only within-person data come from people who cut down rather than stopped.

imprecision.note: 18 against 10 people in the only within-person study, 24 to 30 per group in the others; the absence of deficits in people who had stopped cannot exclude moderate differences.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: The correlation between the fall in use and the gain in category fluency (r = 0.712, 18 people) is within one small selected sample, and the people who used most had most room to improve (regression to the mean is not excluded; card sc_morgan_2004a); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence: neither recovery nor persistence after stopping can be shown with these designs. Status contested, with a debate box: the same research group has published both conclusions (impairments that appear long-lasting, Morgan et al., 2004a; impairments that may be reversible, Morgan et al., 2009 and the 2012 review), each with credible support and a credible critique. Overlapping evidence: the 2009 and 2010 papers are one cohort; the 2004 follow-up is a subset of the two field studies. The narrative review is second-hand and is used only to qualify; its group of 30 people abstinent for at least a year cannot be matched to a primary report.

debate.question: Do the lower memory and thinking scores of people who use ketamine often fade after they cut down or stop?
debate.evidence_yes: People who had stopped scored no lower than either comparison group on any test: 30 people abstinent for at least a month (a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980) in one session (Morgan et al., 2009), and the 23 or 24 of them retested a year later at both sessions, 3 of whom were again using monthly (Morgan et al., 2010b), although 8 had once used daily and the group had used ketamine for longer than the other ketamine groups. In the only study that retested a group of people who had cut down (Morgan et al., 2004a; 18 people whose use fell from 6.45 to 1.61 days a month, beside 10 polydrug controls), category fluency, lower 3 days after a night of use, no longer differed 3 to 4 years later (F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032), errors in sentence judging fell to the controls' level, and the gain in category fluency correlated, by the authors' account, with the reduction in use (r = 0.712) and with time since last use (r = 0.723). Even people who were still using did not get worse on average over a year: their mean spatial working-memory errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and their pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' 88.41% and 89.58% (changes the paper did not test), and their planning improved into the other groups' range (Morgan et al., 2010b). The same authors' narrative review reads these results as showing that memory impairments may be reversible (Morgan & Curran, 2012, second-hand).
debate.evidence_no: In the 18 people who had cut down, immediate story recall and digit-cancellation speed were lower than in the controls at both sessions with no reported improvement, and sentence judging was lower across both sessions although the authors describe it as improving (immediate recall F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047; cancellation 66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 seconds; sentences F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007), which the authors read as long-lasting impairment of episodic memory and possibly of attention (Morgan et al., 2004a); 10 of the 18 had used ketamine within the previous 6 months (editors' arithmetic from the 8 who had not). Over a year, letter fluency fell in the abstinent (17.36 to 15.12) and frequent groups (16.38 to 13.48), which the authors describe as a possible progressive decline (Morgan et al., 2010b). Averaged over both sessions, the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than all other groups and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and abstinent groups, and within that group, by the authors' account, larger increases in the reported amount went with worse changes on both tasks (r = 0.623 and −0.732 as printed), which would fit effects that depend on how much people use.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether ketamine caused the lower scores in the first place: no study tested anyone before they started using, and the frequent groups had less schooling and lower vocabulary-test scores. Whether the same people recover after stopping: the people who had stopped were different people, who had used less before stopping (2.55 days a month, a peak of 11.21, against 20.13 in the frequent group), and only the 3-year follow-up retested a group defined by having cut down; it kept 18 of 57 original ketamine participants (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down, had no group that kept using, and took its first measurement 3 days after a night of use, when after-effects and missed practice may still have lowered scores. The differences that remained were present at the first session and did not change, which fits differences that predate use as well as lasting harm; the improvements in people still using fit practice on tasks with one version and recovery from a poor start as well as anything else. Letter fluency also fell in both control groups, by amounts similar to the abstinent group's. All the studies come from one research group, with self-reported use, testers who knew the groups and 10 to 30 people per group.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). No study read shows whether ketamine's effects on memory and thinking reverse, because none shows what those effects were. What the sources do show is that people who had stopped, after at least a month and usually many months, scored like people who did not use ketamine in two sessions a year apart; that people who were still using did not get worse on average over a year, improving significantly on two tasks and, on average but without a test, on two others; and that in a small, selected follow-up one test caught up after people cut down while story recall and speed did not change. A reading consistent with all of this is that the lower scores of people using ketamine most days include a part that does not outlast heavy use (recent use, after-effects or withdrawal, missed practice) and a part that may have been there before use began, but the studies cannot separate the two. The claims of recovery and the claims of lasting impairment come from the same research group, and both go further than its data.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before regular ketamine use and repeatedly afterwards, with ketamine use and abstinence verified by hair and urine analysis, enough people who continue, cut down and stop to compare them, comparison groups retested on the same schedule with alternate test versions, testers blind to group, and losses reported by baseline scores. None of the sources read reports such a study.
